analysis.one_liner: Establishes a federal right to abortion and requires nearly all health plans to cover it.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; it sat with eight House committees until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write into federal law a right to make decisions about abortion and miscarriage, let people sue governments that violate it, and strike down state restrictions by allowing those lawsuits. It would require almost every health insurance plan — Medicaid, Medicare, employer plans, marketplace plans — to cover abortion care, require federally funded health facilities to provide or refer for it, and create a $350 million annual grant program for clinics, travel costs, provider training, and security. It would also limit immigration enforcement within 2,000 feet of health facilities and expand health coverage for immigrants.
analysis.who_benefits: People who need abortion care, especially those in states with bans or severe restrictions, low-income people on Medicaid, immigrants excluded from coverage today, and patients in detention. Abortion clinics and funds also gain: the bill would fund clinics directly, pay for travel, lodging, and childcare for patients, train new providers, and upgrade clinic security [S3] [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People seeking abortion care, especially in ban states

how_it_helps.text: All persons would have a fundamental right to make decisions about abortion and miscarriage, and governments could not deny or penalize anyone for exercising it; aggrieved individuals could sue federal, state, or local governments to enforce it, and the act would expressly override state immunity and the Religious Freedom Restoration Act [S3] [S2].

Nearly every public and private health plan — including Medicaid, CHIP, Medicare, TRICARE, veterans' care, federal employee plans, marketplace plans, and employer-sponsored plans — would be required to cover abortion services at reimbursement rates sufficient to cover the cost of care, repealing the ACA's restrictions on abortion coverage [S3] [S2].

A $350 million per year grant program would fund clinics providing abortion care in person or by telehealth, training for health professionals, direct payment of patients' care, travel, lodging, and childcare costs, doula services, patient navigators, and clinic construction and security, with priority for medically underserved communities [S3].

Any health care facility receiving federal funds would have to provide or refer patients for all medically appropriate reproductive health care, including abortion; the bill repeals the law that lets health care entities refuse abortion training and referrals, and it would require colleges receiving federal funds to offer medication abortion through student health centers [S3] [S2].

Immigration enforcement actions would be barred within 2,000 feet of any health facility, HIPAA rules would be tightened to block disclosures of reproductive health information to law enforcement and immigration officials, and lawfully present and Deferred Action recipients would gain Medicaid, CHIP, and ACA subsidy eligibility [S3] [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the $350 million annual grant program. Health insurers and employers sponsoring plans would bear new coverage mandates. Hospitals, clinics, pharmacies, and other federally funded health facilities would take on new obligations to provide or arrange abortion care, and institutions of higher education would have to offer medication abortion. State governments enforcing abortion restrictions would face lawsuits they could not assert sovereign immunity against [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, insurers, employers, and federally funded facilities

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes $350 million per year in new federal spending, indefinitely, for grants that include direct payment of individuals' abortion and travel costs [S3].

It removes existing conscience protections by repealing the law that lets health care entities decline abortion training, performance, or referrals, and it conditions all federal health funding on facilities providing or referring for abortion — a real cost and objection for religiously affiliated hospitals and providers [S3].

Mandating abortion coverage across all employer-sponsored and private plans would raise plan costs, and it overrides the accommodation structure the Supreme Court built for employers with religious objections to such coverage [S3].

The bill's enforcement design — letting individuals sue states, abrogating state immunity, and declaring that the act supersedes all other federal law including the Religious Freedom Restoration Act — is an unusually broad preemption of state authority that critics would call constitutionally aggressive [S3].

The 2,000-foot immigration enforcement buffer around health facilities, which covers pharmacies and clinics broadly, would constrain routine immigration enforcement near large parts of populated areas, since the bill's own findings note nearly two-thirds of people live within the 100-mile border zone [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people in states where abortion is banned or severely restricted, the bill's concrete gains — required insurance coverage, paid travel and childcare, more providers, and a lawsuit mechanism against state bans — would be substantial, and the bill's findings document facility closures and provider shortages in those states [S3]. The costs are real but narrower: $350 million a year in federal spending, new coverage and service mandates on insurers, employers, and federally funded facilities including those with religious objections, and a broad assertion of federal power over state abortion law. The bill was written as a maximal statement rather than a compromise, which is one reason it had no support from the chamber's majority.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to eight House committees, then to health subcommittees three times, and no committee ever held a hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ayanna Pressley introduced the Abortion Justice Act of 2023 in the House on June 22, 2023, with 38 cosponsors, all of them Democrats [S1] [S4] [S5].

The bill was referred to eight committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Judiciary, Natural Resources, Armed Services, Veterans' Affairs, Oversight, and Foreign Affairs — a structure that requires broad coordination before any action can move forward [S5] [S1].

The only further actions in the bill's entire history were three referrals to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, in June 2023, September 2023, and December 2024; no hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments enforcing abortion bans keep their restrictions intact, and health insurers, employers, and federally funded facilities avoid the new coverage and service obligations the bill would have imposed. People in states with bans remain without the access the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States with abortion bans; status quo unchanged

sides.party_line_note: All 39 supporters in the House (the sponsor plus 38 cosponsors) were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the House majority that controlled the committees and the floor took no action on it [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill requires nearly every public and private plan, including employer-sponsored and marketplace plans, to cover abortion services at rates sufficient to cover the cost of care. Insurers would gain a newly billable service but take on a new mandate across all lines of business, which is why their interest here runs against the bill's purpose of expanding patient access.

industries.industry: Hospitals and federally funded health facilities
industries.note: Any facility receiving federal funds — including religiously affiliated hospitals, clinics, and pharmacies — would have to provide or refer for abortion care, and the existing conscience law allowing refusal would be repealed. Facilities lose discretion they currently hold, while patients gain guaranteed access.

The bill routes $350 million a year directly to entities providing abortion care: clinic construction, security, broadband, provider training, telehealth, and support services like doulas, escorts, and patient navigators. This is the industry the bill most directly builds up, alongside the patients it serves.

Institutions of higher education receiving federal funds would have to offer medication abortion through student health centers, contracted providers, or telehealth. This creates a new health care obligation for schools; students gain on-campus access.

The bill bars immigration enforcement actions within 2,000 feet of any health facility and restricts sharing of reproductive health data with immigration officials. Enforcement agencies lose operational discretion; immigrants seeking care gain safety from arrest at medical facilities.
